briefing.text: FILE LAYOUT (from headers only, no values analysed): 158807664.node is an AnnData h5ad file despite its extension. X is a CSR sparse matrix stored as float32, shape 966768 nuclei x 32227 genes, with 172,451,705 stored entries. There is no .raw group and layers is empty, so X is the only matrix in the file. obs columns are: sample (categorical, 3 categories), total_counts (float32), n_genes (int64), n_genes_raw (int64), age_group (categorical, 2 categories). var holds only gene names.
briefing.reason: Tells the team how to open the file, that X is the only candidate for the raw matrix, and that two precomputed n_genes-like obs columns exist, which shapes every later check.

briefing.text: PITFALL: X being the only matrix does not prove it holds raw UMI counts; it is float32, and h5ad files often carry normalized, log1p or ambient-corrected values in X. CHECK before thresholding: on X.data confirm every value is integer-valued (np.all(X.data == np.round(X.data))), the minimum is >= 0 (no negatives), the maximum is a plausible UMI count rather than a log-scale value (log1p data tops out around <15), and the row sums of X match obs total_counts. IF all hold: float32 is harmless (integers are exact up to 2^24) and X can be used as the raw matrix. IF non-integer or negative values are found: X is not the raw count matrix, 'count > 0' and 'non-zero' stop being the same definition, and the result should be reported as not computable as specified from X alone (or, if proceeding, use strictly X > 0 and flag it) rather than silently thresholding transformed values.
briefing.reason: The task requires the raw integer count matrix; if X is transformed, the number of nuclei passing n_genes > 1000 may differ or be ill-defined, so this must be verified before anything is counted.

briefing.text: PITFALL: The file already has obs columns n_genes and n_genes_raw. Precomputed columns like these are often stale: scanpy writes obs n_genes only when filter_cells ran, possibly on a different matrix, gene set or processing stage, so the two columns may disagree with each other and with X. CHECK: recompute n_genes from X as (X > 0).sum(axis=1) and compare it elementwise with obs n_genes and with obs n_genes_raw; record how many nuclei differ and how many pass > 1000 under each. IF they mismatch: the task defines n_genes from the raw count matrix, so the value recomputed from a verified-raw X is authoritative; use the obs columns only as a cross-check and report the discrepancy.
briefing.reason: Taking a ready-made obs column as a shortcut could yield a different count than the task's definition; the comparison also serves as an independent check on whether X is really the raw matrix.

briefing.text: PITFALL: The task's threshold is strict (n_genes > 1000), but scanpy's sc.pp.filter_cells(min_genes=N) keeps cells with n_genes >= N, so min_genes=1000 wrongly keeps nuclei with exactly 1000 detected genes. CHECK: count the nuclei with n_genes exactly equal to 1000; if non-zero, the two conventions give different answers. Use an explicit boolean mask n_genes > 1000 (equivalent to min_genes=1001), never min_genes=1000.
briefing.reason: An off-by-one at the boundary changes the integer counts the task asks for, and the default tool convention is the wrong one here.

briefing.text: PITFALL: Any step that removes or alters genes or counts before n_genes is computed changes how many nuclei clear a fixed threshold: sc.pp.filter_genes(min_cells=...), highly-variable-gene subsetting, dropping mitochondrial/ribosomal genes, merging duplicated gene names, normalization, ambient-RNA correction, cell calling, doublet or mito filtering. Tutorial pipelines do several of these by reflex. CHECK: the matrix is still 966768 x 32227 at the moment n_genes is computed and nothing else has been run on it. Apply only the single filter the task asks for (n_genes > 1000) on the untouched matrix with all genes.
briefing.reason: Habitual QC preprocessing would silently change the per-nucleus gene counts and therefore the answer; the task specifies exactly one filter.

briefing.text: PITFALL: In a scipy sparse matrix, X.getnnz(axis=1), X.nnz and np.diff(X.indptr) count STORED entries, which include explicitly stored zeros, so they can overcount genes detected per nucleus. A CSR matrix read from disk can also be non-canonical (duplicate column indices within a row, unsorted indices); duplicates are logically summed, so even (X > 0).sum(axis=1) on an un-deduplicated matrix can count one gene twice. CHECK: (X.data == 0).sum() == 0; X.has_canonical_format is True (or X.nnz is unchanged after X.sum_duplicates()); and np.diff(X.indptr) equals np.asarray((X > 0).sum(axis=1)).ravel(). IF explicit zeros or duplicates are found: run X.sum_duplicates() then X.eliminate_zeros() before counting, and compute n_genes as (X > 0).sum(axis=1) rather than from indptr differences. If neither is present and there are no negative values, the stored-entry count, (X > 0) count and scanpy's n_genes_by_counts agree and can be used to cross-validate one another.
briefing.reason: The fastest way to count genes per nucleus (stored entries per row) is only correct under conditions that must be checked; otherwise n_genes is inflated and nuclei near the threshold are misclassified.

briefing.text: PITFALL: At 966768 x 32227, any densifying operation (X.toarray(), np.asarray(X), X.A, conversion to pandas) needs roughly 125 GB and will crash or tempt subsampling, which makes the count wrong or non-deterministic; anndata backed='r' row-by-row iteration is also reported to leak memory. The sparse matrix has ~172M stored entries (about 2 GB in memory), so load it sparse and keep every operation sparse. IF memory is tight: read X/data, X/indices and X/indptr directly with h5py in row chunks and count data > 0 per row via indptr, over ALL rows - never subsample. Note that the file has a very large number of barcodes relative to its stored entries, so the fraction of nuclei passing the threshold, whatever it turns out to be, is not on its own a reason to doubt or alter the method.
briefing.reason: Determines how the computation can be carried out at all on this file size, and guards against subsampling or 'correcting' the method because the pass rate looks unexpected.

briefing.text: PITFALL: Per-group counts from a pandas categorical can silently lose cells: value_counts drops NaN by default, groupby drops NaN keys and (with observed=False) lists unused categories, and labels may differ in case or whitespace, so Adult + Aged may not equal total. CHECK: adata.obs['age_group'].isna().sum() == 0; the categories are exactly 'Adult' and 'Aged'; after filtering, Adult + Aged == total; use value_counts(dropna=False). Also cross-tabulate sample x age_group (there are 3 samples) to confirm each sample maps to a single age group. IF unlabelled or oddly labelled nuclei exist: report total as all nuclei passing the filter and state how those nuclei were handled rather than letting them vanish.
briefing.reason: The answer needs three mutually consistent integers; label problems would make the Adult/Aged split wrong or inconsistent with the total.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume X is the raw UMI matrix. This was tested, not just assumed: values are non-negative integers stored as float32, row sums equal obs total_counts, and per-row non-zero counts equal both obs n_genes and obs n_genes_raw for every barcode. The file has no .raw group and an empty layers group (confirmed from the headers), so there is no other candidate matrix.

Both teams treat every one of the 966768 barcodes as a 'nucleus' in scope, with no cell calling, doublet or mito step before the threshold. The task lists a single filter, so this follows the text; neither team tested an alternative because the task gives none.
Both teams count one gene per matrix column. I checked the headers: the 32227 var names are all distinct, so counting columns and counting distinct gene names are the same thing.
Both teams assume each barcode is one independent record. The 966768 obs names are all distinct (team B checked; confirmed from the headers).
unused_evidence: obs 'sample' (3M, 21M1, 21M2) is not needed for the requested numbers; both teams used it only to confirm each sample maps to one age group. Ignoring it cannot change the counts.

obs 'total_counts', 'n_genes' and 'n_genes_raw' were used as cross-checks by both teams and match the recomputed values exactly. The existence of two identical gene-count columns is odd but harmless here, since both equal the value recomputed from X.
uns holds only a platform key string; var has no columns beyond gene names; obsm, obsp, varm, varp and layers are empty. Nothing else in the file bears on the question.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A named the strict '>' versus '>=' convention. Resolved: it counted the nuclei sitting exactly on the threshold (11), showed the two conventions differ by that amount, and used the strict mask the task states.
Team B named the assumption that X is raw. Resolved as far as the file allows: integer values, matching obs columns including one named n_genes_raw, and no other matrix in the file.

Team B recorded no pitfalls checked and did not report the boundary count or a check for duplicate column indices within a row. This is covered by team A, which verified a canonical CSR with no explicit zeros and no duplicate indices; team B's total equals team A's strict-threshold total, not the '>=' total, so team B's mask was strict too.
second_readings: 'n_genes > 1000' could be mistaken for the common min_genes=1000 ('>=') convention; the task writes '>' explicitly, and both teams followed it.

'total' could in principle mean something other than Adult plus Aged if some barcodes had no age label; team A confirmed there are no missing codes and the two groups sum to the total, so the readings coincide.
'genes with count > 0' could mean distinct gene symbols rather than matrix columns; gene names are unique, so the readings coincide.
I found no second reading of the quantity, group, scale or time point that gives a different number on this file.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed answer highly. The task is a fully specified deterministic count, both teams computed it from the full untouched matrix and matched the file's own precomputed columns, and each named weak point was checked on the data; my own look at the file headers (single matrix, unique gene names, unique barcodes, two age categories) turned up no unused evidence or alternative reading that could move the numbers, so I have no question worth a team's time.
